Positive: event id 80 (item 62, LORA firing) and event id 138 (item 50, TITAN $192M) are clean, single, well-attributed events with correct parties/customer/program fields -- so the extraction pipeline clearly can produce correct output, the failures above are not universal.

5 of 6 golden investigations (jobs 46, 47, 48, 70, 91) ended outcome='not_found' with confidence 0.0-0.3 -- the deep-search agent did not answer the underlying question for the large majority of this sample. Job 91 (the 2x-budget re-run of job 86, item 1352/Reaper) still failed after 30 queries, 10 pages and 4 rounds.

Job 86 (item 1352, 'verify the Reaper-successor-timeline report') is worse than an honest miss: it returned a substantive, confident-sounding answer entirely about Elbit's MOSP 5000 payload -- a system never mentioned in the question -- and was only flagged wrong by a retroactive relevance_check correction dated after the fact ('verdict: no ... retroactive correction, 2026-09-06'), i.e. the system shipped an off-topic answer and caught it after the fact rather than before.

Mitigating factor the rubric explicitly rewards: when the agent does fail, it is honest about it -- job 46/47/48/70 all explicitly say 'לא נמצא מידע מספק' and describe concrete search attempts (specific query strings, number of pages/rounds) rather than fabricating a plausible-sounding answer. This honesty is real and should be credited, but it does not substitute for actually answering the golden questions.

Net effect: on the 'does it answer the question' criterion the golden sample is failing 5/6 (83%); on the 'honest about gaps' criterion it is succeeding on those same 5; the 1 apparent 'success' (job 86, later corrected to job 91 which itself failed) shows the one time it produced a confident narrative it was for the wrong topic.

Live-tested all 8 golden questions against POST /api/ask on the running server (127.0.0.1:8765). Only 4/8 (Q1 XM30, Q2 Iron Beam, Q3 Greece LORA, Q4 DROIC) returned an answer within 120s per call; Q5 (Skyranger vs. Israeli C-UAS), Q6 (AUSA 2026 relevance), Q7 (US EO/IR RFI) and Q8 (Elbit SPECTRO ISR maturity) all hit the 120s client timeout with zero output -- a 50% non-response rate in this run (GPU-shared environment, per docs/QA_CONTINUOUS_LOOP.md sec 4, so some slowness is expected, but a flat timeout with no partial-answer fallback on half the fixed question set is a real user-facing gap).

Of the 4 answers received, 0/4 contain any inline [n] citation marker even though a citations array was returned alongside each -- this directly fails the D5 deterministic rubric line 'ציטוטים [n] תקפים'. All 4/4 also render raw Markdown syntax (##, **bold**, '*   ' bullet lists) rather than the plain-text-with-citations format the product calls for -- a clean, 100%-reproducible violation of 'ללא markdown גולמי'.

Q4 (DROIC trend) appears to hallucinate corporate attribution: it names 'Leonardo DRS', 'Omnisys' and 'Tobyhanna Army Depot' as developing a technology called 'RAFT-DVC' inside an invented 'FlexibleFusion' platform, when the actual retrieved source (citation n=3) is an arXiv academic paper titled 'RAFT-DVC: Resolution-Aware Machine Learning-Based Digital Volume Correlation' -- an academic algorithm, not a named defense-company product line. A senior analyst would flag this as fabricated.

Q2 (Iron Beam contract details) opens with a header framing the answer as 'רפאל's first US Army laser production contract', then spends most of the response describing the AeroVironment/Locust X3 E-HEL contract (a different company, different program, no connection to Rafael or Iron Beam) before a brief closing caveat admits the sources don't actually cover Iron Beam. The structure invites the reader to misread AeroVironment's contract as Rafael's.

Q1 and Q3 are directionally reasonable and readable (Q3's Greece/LORA answer correctly covers the David's Sling/Barak MX/Spyder layered stack and the Turkey-rivalry framing) but Q3 is highly repetitive (the same 'strategic opportunity for Israeli industry' point is restated near-verbatim under 3 different headers), and Q1 pulled at least 2 clearly irrelevant citations into its citation list (a DJI/FCC drone story and a generic C4I product release, neither about XM30).

output/reports/weekly_2026-09-05.md contains literal test/placeholder text shipped as if it were real analyst output: the executive summary reads 'זהו תקציר בדיקה קצר' ('this is a short test summary'), the trend section reads 'תיאור מגמה' ('trend description'), two section headers are literally titled 'placeholder air_defense' / 'placeholder airborne_pods' with body text 'תיאור כללי' ('general description'), and the entire 'מבט קדימה' (forward-look) section is the single sentence 'להערכתנו זהו מבחן' ('in our assessment, this is a test'). This is the single worst finding in the sample -- a production weekly report with no real narrative content at all in its most important sections.

The weekly report's 'סיכום מטא שבועי' section is dominated by ~80 lines of feedback-calibration log entries, the large majority of which are exact duplicate contradictory pairs for the same headline flipping red<->yellow and back (e.g. the 'כשה-AI יכול להתחזות' item alone appears roughly 30 times alternating direction) -- reads as a logging bug dumped into a user-facing report, not a curated summary of user feedback.

output/reports/daily_2026-09-06.md is more honest about its own failure but equally empty of narrative: the exec summary section states outright that the draft failed citation QA and was dropped entirely ('הטיוטה הטקסטואלית של הדוח לא עברה את בדיקת האזכורים... ולכן הושמטה במלואה'), leaving only deterministic tables. Per docs/QA_CONTINUOUS_LOOP.md's explicit ask to 'note if the daily is tables-only and why' -- confirmed: it is tables-only, and the reason is a citation-QA gate rejecting the generated prose outright rather than repairing/regenerating it.

The deterministic per-sentence citation check on daily_2026-09-06.md trivially 'passes' (0 uncited sentences) only because there are zero narrative sentences to check -- a good illustration of why the citation gate alone cannot certify 'coherent, analyst-grade' output.

Positive: the tender-forecast table's rationale prose (in both daily and weekly) is coherent, cites concrete item ids, and reasons plausibly about which platforms will need which EO/IR payload -- this piece of the report is doing real work even while the surrounding narrative sections are broken.

Graded the most recently generated patent survey by file mtime: output/reports/patent_survey_Anduril_Lattice_counter-UAS_EO_IR_optical_tracking_patents_2026-09-06.md (08:42, later than the DROIC survey at 08:25 that round_0_auto.json happened to score). The 'ציר זמן שנתי' (annual timeline) and 'קודי CPC מובילים' (top CPC codes) tables -- both rubric-required for a technology map -- are present as headers but completely empty (zero rows) in this survey.

There is no per-patent 'advance' description anywhere in the document: every patent row has only a title, a flat value-score of 10 (except the one Anduril patent at 12), and a Google Patents link -- no sentence anywhere explains what each patent actually claims or how it maps to a product. This fails the rubric's explicit 'per-patent advance' and 'business chain (technology->product->program)' requirements for all but the single correctly-assigned patent.

The narrative sections ('נוף הפטנטים', 'פרופיל מקצה') openly admit 'לא זוהו פטנטים ספציפיים של Anduril' and then pivot entirely away from patents into a recap of recent news events (TITAN contract, Hermeus partnership, Norkin appointment) that are unrelated to patent activity -- this is a competitive-intelligence news brief mislabeled as a patent survey, not a technology-landscape analysis.

The one correctly-identified Anduril patent (Lattice mesh) is real and relevant, and the missing-API-key caveat is honestly disclosed ('הזן EPO_OPS_KEY/PATENTSVIEW_API_KEY... לכיסוי מלא') -- so the survey is honest about its own limits, but that does not make the deliverable usable as a technology map.

Tenders: the entire `tenders` table has exactly 5 rows and ZERO have status='open' (verified by direct query). The 5 rows ingested are all `status='closed'`, several with deadlines from 2015-2016 and 2023, and even the most recent (id 30, Finnish EO/IR RFI) closed on 2025-10-01, before the current date (2026-09-06). This directly fails the rubric's explicit 'רק פתוחים/עדכניים' (only open/current) requirement -- the tenders feed currently surfaces nothing actionable at all.

Conferences: strong. 15 rows checked all have real, plausible dates, sensible status values (confirmed/estimated), and match config/watchlist.yaml's conferences_seed (organizer, city, month) which per docs/MODULES.md was live-verified against real conference sites -- this is the one clearly solid sub-piece of D9.

Tender forecasts: structurally reasonable (7 rows, each anchored to a plausible payload_need/platform pair with a window_from/window_to and a likelihood in [0.5, 0.8]), and the rationale prose in the daily report cites concrete item ids. But the prose is templated across rows ('זוהו X אירועים... פלטפורמה זו נזקקת בדרך כלל ל-Y') rather than differentiated per forecast, and forecasts are a proxy for tenders, not a replacement for the empty real-tenders pipeline.

Net: the part of D9 users would actually check for actionable near-term opportunities (open tenders) is empty and stale; the parts that work well (conferences) are calendar/reference data, not opportunity data.
